_comment: Backfill for r20261113-1630 (bench 6: r20261113-1351's build and configuration, the always-on form of the vote fix with the arm file final, on Hyperdisk Balanced at 50,000 provisioned IOPS), published with: bash benchmark/launch/launch.sh tasks/bench6/r20261113-1630/bench6-run2b.env bundle --compare r20261113-1351 --backfill benchmark/report/backfill/2026-11-13-bench6-always-50k.json. Sources: tasks/bench6-report-r20261113-1351.md sections 1 to 8 and benchmark/private/bench6-r20261113-2118/A7/comparison.md for every statement and figure (figure-by-figure notes in tasks/checkpoint-bench7-P1.md); the run's own manifest.json for recovery.node, recovery.killed_utc and recovery.restarted_utc (the chaos block's ts fields, the same ones kpis.recovery reads, so the merge is silent) and for fleet (machine type, zones, disk, blasters). recovery.rejoined_utc, recovery.catch_up_secs and recovery.failed_reports are null: make_bundle computes them from the tn_node_mode series and the batch-seal failure counter, which the sources above do not give; the node log's kill-to-active times are in the caveats instead. Written 2026-11-14.
title: The always-on vote fix on Hyperdisk Balanced at 50,000 IOPS
summary: We repeated r20261113-1351 with one change: each node's Hyperdisk Balanced disk was provisioned at 50,000 IOPS instead of bench 5's 20,000. The build (2df831e3c), the four switches (the vote fix in its always-on form, the voter's lock-wait fix, the epoch-record state check and the database's random-access hint), the fleet, the load and the chaos plan were the same. With the disk off its limit, average chain throughput with all ten generators running was 7,329.0 tx/s, 112.5 % above bench 5's 3,448.7 tx/s and 37.7 % above r20261113-1351's 5,322.1 (derived), and it held through the blast at 7,077 to 7,684 tx/s in each five minutes. The median time until a generator saw its receipt fell from 12.99 s to 8.32 s; the floor stayed at 1.63 s. The disk no longer binds: the median validator's disk ran 24,837 writes a second, half its limit, and the database commit fell from 74.2 to 22.4 µs per transaction. The engine binds instead. In this build executing and persisting a consensus output run in series, and the costliest engine (validator-01, 136.9 µs per transaction) has a capacity of 7,287 tx/s, the fleet's executed rate. The vote fix did not hold at this disk. Through the light blasts and the first 120 s of the load it certified as well as at 20,000 IOPS, but over the load blast four validators lost certification: validator-06 certified 44.5 % of its own headers, validator-10 68.2 %, validator-02 78.6 % and validator-09 95.8 %, while the other six stayed at 99.9 to 100 %. The always-on form names its author's executed tip minus 8 outputs. Once the disk no longer gave every engine the same cost, the engines spread by 18 to 45 outputs, so a fast author named blocks that four or five voters had not executed yet, and those voters answered after the author had moved on to its next header. It is a liveness and throughput problem, not a safety one: no node forked or halted. More accepted transactions landed only after a resend (133,975 resends on eight generators; 14,928 never landed), the reordering tracked as issue #1807. Validator-05 rejoined once, 21 min 30.2 s after its kill. This run is one of four in one program, one node build with two forms of the vote fix on two disks: the always-on form as r20261113-1351 (20,000 IOPS) and r20261113-1630 (50,000 IOPS), the adaptive form as r20261113-2118 (20,000 IOPS) and r20261114-0000 (50,000 IOPS). Across them the form changed neither throughput nor what binds; the always-on form certified slightly more own headers at 20,000 IOPS, neither form held certification at 50,000 IOPS (the adaptive run certified more), the adaptive form's senders paid more on both disks through the same reordering (issue #1807), and which form goes upstream is not decided.

evidence_detail: Commit 2df831e3c is the head of the branch bench/bench6-2026-11, built for this benchmark: a base commit 165e3fe01 plus 98 commits, in which every fix for bench 5's concerns is a node switch, off by default. The twelve switches are quorum_exec_block (the vote fix, whose form the setting quorum_exec_block_starved_rounds picks), vote_queue_fix, epoch_record_state_check, mdbx_random_advice, mdbx_no_writemap, sealed_tx_keep, digest_dedupe, recovery_threads, epoch_close_task_drain, pipelined_persist, rpc_admission_backlog_outputs and parent_grace. A node logs its switches at every start ('node switches') and exports them as tn_node_switch. The image was named by registry digest (adiri@sha256:874537ff…852745) and ran all four runs of this program unchanged.

fleet.label: c3-highcpu-8 + Hyperdisk Balanced at 50,000 IOPS (c3-hdb), ten regions, validator-05 in Ashburn

load.placement: one blaster per validator, in that validator's zone, sending only to it

methodology: All four runs of this program used one node image, built from the branch bench/bench6-2026-11 at commit 2df831e3c (a base commit 165e3fe01 plus 98 commits), with sub-second timestamps from genesis, and named by registry digest (adiri@sha256:874537ff…852745). Nothing was rebuilt between the runs. Every fix in that build is a node switch, off by default; a node logs its switches at every start ('node switches') and exports them as the metric tn_node_switch. The load generator was built from tn-transaction-generator commit 62bbd5f.

The vote fix is the switch quorum_exec_block. Instead of its own newest executed block, a proposer names in each header a block that a quorum of validators should already have executed; a voter signs only after it finds the named block in its own chain. The setting quorum_exec_block_starved_rounds picks the form. With 0, the always-on form, every header takes the quorum value over the author's own executed tip and the blocks its parent headers named, capped at the own tip and never more than 8 outputs behind it (the floor); in practice nearly every header named the author's tip minus 8 outputs. With 4, the adaptive form, a header names the author's own tip until one of the author's headers is cancelled uncertified; the author then uses the always-on rule inside a starved window of up to 128 rounds, and afterwards tries its own tip again.

Three more switches were on in all four runs: vote_queue_fix (the voter's lock wait), epoch_record_state_check (a check of the closing state when an epoch record is built) and mdbx_random_advice (the MDBX database's random-access hint over the whole file from the first start). The other eight stayed at their defaults: mdbx_no_writemap, sealed_tx_keep, digest_dedupe, recovery_threads, epoch_close_task_drain, pipelined_persist, rpc_admission_backlog_outputs and parent_grace. The switch set came from an arm file applied at deployment, before the nodes' coordinated start: no arm walk, no cache eviction and no restart before the load.

Each run created ten validators and one observer on c3-highcpu-8 (8 vCPU, 16 GiB), each node with one 100 GB Hyperdisk Balanced disk for the root and the data directory at 800 MiB/s, provisioned at 20,000 IOPS (bench 5's disk) or 50,000 IOPS. One validator ran in each of bench 5's ten regions (Los Angeles, London, Sydney, Tokyo, Ashburn, the Netherlands, Singapore, Hong Kong, Seoul and Mumbai), the observer in Los Angeles. Epochs last 1,200 s.

Each run had three blasts. Ten generators on e2-standard-2, one per validator in that validator's zone and sending only to it, ran blast 0, the floor, with 8 senders each and up to 16 transactions in flight per sender (8 x 16); blast 1 with 600 senders and a window of 4 (600 x 4, at most 24,000 in flight); and blast 2, the load blast, with 600 senders and a window of 16 (600 x 16, at most 96,000 in flight) and phases of 120 s warm-up, 2,400 s mixed load and 180 s cool-down, the shape of bench 5's load blast.

The chaos plan was bench 5's, inside blast 2: validator-05's container was killed with SIGKILL shortly before an epoch boundary and held down for 300 s, so the outage crossed the boundary; then it was started, and the observer was restarted 300 s after that. Generator 05 sends only to validator-05 and does not fail over to another endpoint, so it is cut off for the outage and for as long as its validator follows the chain afterwards.

Headline figures keep bench 5's definitions and code; bench 5's throughput, latency and landing figures quoted on these pages were recomputed exactly from bench 5's own generator documents with the same code, while its certification, disk, stage and rejoin figures come from bench 5's report or from this program's reading of bench 5's logs and model. Throughput is the chain's transactions per second over the window in which all ten generators ran, with the outage and generator 05 inside it. Time to seen runs from submission until the generator saw the receipt, from the generators' summed histograms (the bundle method); time to land is to the block's timestamp, in whole seconds, so about 0.5 s low. Own-header certification is the share of a validator's own headers that were certified, over blast 2's mixed phase unless another window is named.

The analysis read every node's whole main log (the node's stderr file was not pulled) and the node metrics exported from Prometheus before each teardown. The comparison of the two forms ran the same scripts on both runs of a disk and reproduced the always-on runs' figures.

Against r20261113-1351 only the disk changed: 50,000 provisioned IOPS instead of 20,000, at the same 800 MiB/s. The arm file final, the image and the generator are the same, so the always-on form ran here too.

Before the nodes started, the harness probed each host: the same kernel (7.0.0-1017-gcp) and read-ahead (128 KB) on every node, and an fsync probe median of 1,006 µs, with validator-06 flagged slow (1,226 µs). Before the first blast it found, on all eleven nodes, the four switches on and the rest off, the random-access hint covering the whole database map, and the database's prefault writes at 0.830 of newly allocated pages.

Times are UTC on 13 November. Deployment ran from 16:30:48 to 17:14:11, with the arm in place at 16:50:28. The mixed phases ran 17:24:45-17:31:02 (blast 0), 17:37:13-17:43:22 (blast 1) and 17:55:32-18:36:19 (blast 2). Epoch boundaries fell at 17:42:19, 18:02:19 and 18:22:19. Validator-05 was killed at 18:21:20 and started at 18:26:20, and the observer was restarted at 18:31:20.

All ten generators ended every blast with rc 0, every fund was complete, and no generator started more than 2 s late; the run's log records no friction. The teardown deleted all 12 instances (18:56:08-19:11:16); the fleet was up 2 h 40 min from the deploy's launch to the teardown's end. The results directory holds 651 files, 2.67 GB, and the export before the teardown holds 382 node metrics (21,950 series).
caveats: Against r20261113-1351 only the disk changed. Throughput rose from 5,322.1 to 7,329.0 tx/s, the best 60 s from 7,327.4 to 8,256.4 tx/s, blocks a second from 23.70 to 27.72 and transactions landed in blast 2 from 14,620,952 to 19,484,670. Time to land p50/p95/p99 went from 0.68/14.66/61.91 s to 0.86/3.53/31.45 s, and time to seen p50/p95 from 12.99/30.89 s to 8.32/25.74 s. The mean time to seen fell 4.54 s: the engine queue gave 6.05 s, partly given back by the wait for the validator's own execution (+1.28 s) and the pool wait (+0.41 s). Against bench 5 (r20261107-1504) throughput is 112.5 % higher, but bench 5 was bound by the bytes its disk wrote and this run by its engines.

Generator 05 was silent for 38 % of the headline window (65 % in bench 5), and the other nine generators carried 7,203.1 tx/s. The rate held through the blast: 7,342.9 tx/s in the first five-minute bucket, 7,683.8 at its best, and 7,077.1 in the eighth, 8 % under the best.

The disk no longer binds. Over blast 2 the median validator, validator-05 aside, ran 24,837 device writes a second (0.497 of 50,000), 5.1 KiB each, 3.41 writes per transaction, 123 MiB/s on the mean against 800 (busiest second 260 MiB/s), and the device was busy 0.17 of the time against 0.39 at 20,000 IOPS. The database commit took 22.4 µs per transaction against 74.2. Device bytes per page byte were 1.156 to 1.170 on the validators and 1.062 on the observer.

The engine binds instead. Per executed transaction it spent 133.9 µs: execute 87.7, persist 44.5 (save 21.9, commit 22.4) and announce 0.75. Against 20,000 IOPS the task fell 53.3 µs per transaction, 51.8 of it in the commit, and outputs grew 50 %. Execute is now the larger part (639 of 975 busy ms a second): state root 42.4 µs, EVM 27.5, commit 22.4, save_blocks 21.9, finish 16.6. The fleet's engines were 975 ms busy each second with the queue at its cap in 42 % of samples (3 to 98 % by validator). Validator-01, the costliest engine at 136.9 µs, ran 997 ms a second busy with a flat backlog of 14 to 18 outputs, and its capacity, 7,287 tx/s, is the fleet's executed rate (7,277 to 7,293 on the others). Validator-06, the cheapest at 130.6 µs, idled 50 ms a second. What held the input at validator-01's capacity was not measured; the pool held 477 transactions on the median validator, so it was not the pool.

An estimate made before this run put the ceiling at this disk at 8,600 to 10,300 tx/s. It was built on the arm-walk run's execute cost alone and left out the persist, which runs in series in this build. With the persist included, the same execute costs give 6,161 to 6,969 tx/s and this run's own costs 7,469 tx/s at full busy, against 7,287 measured; with the persist free, 11,397 tx/s. These figures are arithmetic, not runs. The persist is busy about 324 ms of each second here, so pipelined persist has room at this disk, but it was off and is untested at 50,000 IOPS, and it lowers each engine's cost, which may widen or narrow the spread behind the certification loss.

Certification held through both light blasts, the warm-up and blast 2's first 120 s (99.97 % of the fleet's own headers in that window). Over the mixed phase the fleet certified 88.26 % (7,025 of 59,826 own headers lost): validator-06 44.5 % (its lowest five-minute bucket 18.7 %), validator-10 68.2 %, validator-02 78.6 %, validator-09 95.8 %, the other six 99.9 to 100 %. Before the kill validator-05 answered 'superseded' to 33,414 vote requests and voted 2,908 times, validator-01 20,507 and 16,153 times. The fleet refused 265 votes as execution-behind and answered 'superseded' 93,730 times, and the median round slowed from 353 to 374 ms.

The mechanism, step by step. The always-on form names its author's tip minus 8 executed outputs on 97 to 99 % of headers, because its inputs are the parents' earlier picks and the floor is the only way up. Validator-06 ran about 18 outputs ahead of validator-01 and 45 ahead of validator-05, and 7 to 9 ahead of validators 04 and 02 (rounds converted to outputs at two rounds per output, an inference), so the block a fast author named was one that four or five voters had not executed. A voter without the block waits up to 1 s; the author's next header comes about 360 ms later, so the voter answers 'superseded', and neither that nor 'behind' is a vote. With four voters out a header cannot certify (none of validator-06's 1,643 headers with five or fewer timely votes did); with exactly six it certified only when the six round trips fit inside the round: 99 % for validator-09 in Seoul, whose six are near, 39 % for validator-06 and 48 % for validator-10. The spread came from the engines: with the disk off its limit each ran at its own cost (130.6 to 136.9 µs per transaction), validators 01, 04 and 05 kept full queues while validator-06 drained to about one output, and validators 05 and 01 fell steadily behind. At 20,000 IOPS the disk had given every engine the same cost (187.0 to 187.3 µs). The round-trip step is inferred, because vote arrival is not logged.

Safety held: a vote is signed only after the voter finds the named block number and hash in its own chain, the subscriber checks each committed leader's block the same way, and no node logged an unexpected execution result, a fork or a halt. Recomputing the rule on this run's measured tips before the kill, with rounds and leaders held fixed, gives validator-06 40.5 % at the floor of 8 as run, 90.4 % with a floor of 16 and 100 % with a floor of 32 (validator-10: 52.2, 80.5 and 99.7 %), for a named block about 6, 12 or 24 s old; a quorum over fresh tips gives validator-06 60.0 %, and the switch off 2.7 %. This is arithmetic, not a result: a different floor would move the tips and rounds it holds fixed, and no run has tested one. An older named block costs detection time, not detection: a diverged node is caught up to N outputs later, about 24 s at N = 32.

130,554 landings were seen 300 s or more after submission: 120,778 gap resends and 9,776 that generator 05's scanner saw late. 133,975 transactions were resent after the generators' gap check, by eight generators, and 14,928 never landed after the 180-s tail scan, 7,674 of them sent to validator-02 and 5,715 to validator-06; landed over accepted was 99.9232 %. The faster disk multiplied the always-on form's resends by 4.4 against r20261113-1351. The mechanism is the same in all four runs of this program and is tracked as issue #1807: when an own header is cancelled or committed late, its batches are queued again behind batches a newer own header already carried, so the sender's later transactions are skipped at execution as 'nonce too high', sit in no pool, and land only after the generator resends its window at its 300-s gap check. The pool switches sealed_tx_keep and digest_dedupe were off in all four runs; whether they change this cost was not measured in these runs (in the earlier arm-walk run, sealed_tx_keep with three other switches on left no gap resends, a reading confounded with the other switches and an epoch boundary).

Validator-05 rejoined once and held: 21 min 30.2 s from the kill to active and 16 min 30.1 s from its start, by the node's log. It replayed epoch 5 under load at 1.180 outputs a second while the chain made 1.243, so its deficit grew to 585 outputs until the load ended, by the same rejoin rule as in r20261113-1351. While it followed, its RPC refused every transaction; generator 05 dropped 314,010 sends and landed nothing for the last 899 s of the blast. In the five minutes before the kill generator 05 landed only 131 to 163 tx/s against the others' median of 639 to 917, following its validator's backlog. Validator-05 refused 17,586 votes as inactive and signed neither epoch record after its kill. Nineteen minutes before the kill, at the 18:02:19 close, it had been demoted twice for 4.05 s in all ('epoch_behind'), with one failed promotion. The observer followed the chain again 8.0 s after its restart.

All six epoch closes certified on one record hash and one closing block on every node. The close inside the outage (18:22:19) is the thinnest close of the arm-walk run, r20261113-1351 and this run: with validator-05 down and validators 01 and 02 still draining 15-output backlogs, the seventh vote went out at 11.30 s and no eighth came, with a commit gap of 10.31 s. Validator-01 was the late validator at every loaded close. 'failed to reach quorum on epoch close' fired once, on validator-04 72.79 s after the 18:02:19 close, on a record the network had certified. No test in this build (2df831e3c) crosses an epoch close with the always-on form.

No hard check fired: no halt, fork, unexpected execution result, fatal database error or panic in any node's whole main log. The nodes logged 73,535 warnings and 17,833 errors, driven by the outage (20,875 dial failures), validator-05 as a follower (16,912 certificate-manager warnings to the blast's end and 7,569 'processed certificate that is too new' errors after it) and the observer's sync retries. Against r20261113-1351, 'failed to get vote for header … Canceled' rose from 45 to 1,132 lines and QuorumRejected from 39 to 142, both tied to the certification loss. The node's stderr file was not pulled.
The pre-start fsync probe flagged validator-06 as slow; it was the cheapest engine, so the flag did not predict the slow node.

The adaptive form on this disk (r20261114-0000) certified more own headers (94.82 % against 88.26 %), but inside its starved windows its fast proposers named the same floor-8 block, it still lost certification, and its senders paid more. With one run per form, the form cannot be told apart from which validators lagged.
The teardown's provenance check warns 'node startup provenance mismatch' in all four runs: each node's start during staging ran before the arm file was applied. It is known and not a finding.

Not measured: when a vote reaches its author (not logged), what held the input at validator-01's capacity, why blast 1's execute cost (112 to 113 µs per transaction) exceeded blast 2's (88 to 90), what the rise of save_blocks is made of, a second cause of slower rounds within the blast (0.352 to 0.392 s with almost no rounds waiting for under-held headers), and a deeper floor in a real run.

Each configuration ran once (one run per form and disk), so run-to-run variation is not measured. The form of the vote fix is not decided: at 20,000 IOPS the always-on form certified a little more and cost the senders less, at 50,000 IOPS neither form held certification, and the floor's depth has been tested only as arithmetic. A further run of both forms is planned on a build of the newer upstream main branch, which uses a different execution storage engine (tn-lmdb) than these runs (MDBX), with a candidate fix for issue #1807 added; its result is not known.
